focused.title: ZJIT: Compile exception handlers
focused.body:
## Summary

This change lets ZJIT compile code for frames selected by `jit_exec_exception()`.

ZJIT now:

- Compiles the active catch continuation at the current `cfp->pc`.
- Restores the existing frame locals and operand stack at each exception entry.
- Uses a patchable PC guard chain to select the correct entry.
- Compiles all observed exception PCs into one shared ISEQ version.
- Uses generic types for exception-entry locals and stack values.
- Reuses a compiled entry when runtime values change.
- Refines the known `fixnum_inc` input before `FixnumAdd`.
- Continues eligible caller frames in ZJIT after a handler returns.
- Includes exception versions in invalidation and garbage collection.
- Uses the interpreter when ZJIT cannot enter a frame safely.

## Why exception entry needs a separate path

A normal ZJIT entry starts a method at its normal bytecode entry.

An exception entry resumes an existing frame after the interpreter unwinds the stack.
At this point, `cfp->pc` points to a catch-table continuation.
The frame already contains locals and operand-stack values.

Before this change, every ZJIT exception entry returned to the interpreter:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    EXCEPTION["Selected exception continuation"] --> STUB["Counter stub"]
    STUB --> QUNDEF["Return Qundef"]
    QUNDEF --> VM["Run the interpreter"]
```

The new path enters HIR at the selected continuation:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    EXCEPTION["Selected exception continuation"] --> DISPATCH["PC guard chain"]
    DISPATCH --> ENTRY["ExceptionEntryPoint"]
    ENTRY --> HIR["Run continuation HIR"]
```

## Lazy PC dispatch

An ISEQ has one `jit_exception` function pointer.
Its catch table can contain many continuation PCs.

ZJIT installs a patchable guard chain behind `jit_exception`.
The first observed PC creates the first guard and exception function.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CALL["jit_exception"] --> PC8{"cfp->pc == PC 8?"}
    PC8 -->|Yes| ENTRY8["Version 1: entry 8"]
    PC8 -->|No| STUB["Compile stub"]
```

A new PC reaches the compile stub.
ZJIT then compiles one function with every observed PC.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CALL["jit_exception"] --> PC8{"cfp->pc == PC 8?"}
    PC8 -->|Yes| ENTRY8["Shared version: entry 8"]
    PC8 -->|No| PC13{"cfp->pc == PC 13?"}
    PC13 -->|Yes| ENTRY13["Shared version: entry 13"]
    PC13 -->|No| STUB["Compile stub"]
```

`ExceptionEntryGuard::regenerate()` connects an old guard to the new guard.
`ExceptionEntryGuard::retarget()` changes a successful branch to the newest function version.

The guard chain remains stable after recompilation.
The old guards enter the newest shared function.

## Shared HIR version

This example has two `break` continuations:

```ruby
def pick(left)
  if left
    1.times { break :left }
  else
    1.times { break :right }
  end
end
```

The catch table selects instruction 8 for `:left` and instruction 13 for `:right`.

ZJIT creates one `ExceptionEntryPoint` block for each observed instruction.
Each block restores an existing interpreter frame.

The entry block:

1. Loads locals from `EP`.
2. Moves the ZJIT `SP` register to the operand-stack bottom.
3. Loads operand values from `SP`.
4. Passes the restored `FrameState` to the continuation block.

`IseqCodePtrs::exception_entry_ptrs` stores the machine address for each PC.
All entries from one compilation reference the same `IseqVersion`.

`--zjit-dump-hir` prints this HIR without snapshot fields:

```text
fn pick@-e:1:
bb1():
  EntryPoint exception(8, stack_size=1)
  v2:CPtr = GetEP 0
  v3:BasicObject = LoadField v2, :left@-0x18
  v4:CPtr = LoadSP
  v5:BasicObject = LoadField v4, :stack[0]@0x0
  CheckInterrupts
  Return v5
bb5():
  EntryPoint exception(13, stack_size=1)
  v10:CPtr = GetEP 0
  v11:BasicObject = LoadField v10, :left@-0x18
  v12:CPtr = LoadSP
  v13:BasicObject = LoadField v12, :stack[0]@0x0
  CheckInterrupts
  Return v13
```

Both entry blocks use `BasicObject` for the local and the operand-stack value.
The function has no entry `GuardType` instructions.
Both entries continue inside one HIR function.

## Generic entry types

An exception entry has no compiled predecessor that can supply reliable value types.
The interpreter can reach one continuation with different local and stack values.

Using current runtime types would require a `GuardType` for every local and stack value.
Different values at the same PC would then cause guard exits and additional function versions.

`liquid-render` reaches one `Array#each` continuation through paths with incompatible stack types.
Generic entry values keep the merged HIR valid until an operation refines or guards its input.

The implementation records the entry shape without speculative value types:

```rust
pub struct ExceptionEntrySpec {
    pub insn_idx: u16,
    pub stack_size: u8,
    pub value_types: Vec<Type>,
}
```

`capture_exception_entry()` fills `value_types` with `BasicObject`.
The list contains all locals, then all operand-stack values.

This design has three effects:

- An entry does not guard each current Ruby value.
- The same PC reuses one compiled target when values change.
- A new PC still causes compilation of a new shared function version.

Some operations can exit when the handler has no profile data.
This behavior is preferable to specialization on values that can change at the same PC.

## `fixnum_inc` refinement

Ruby uses `fixnum_inc` inside methods such as `Array#each`.
Its numeric input starts at zero and remains a Fixnum after each increment.

Generic exception-entry types hide this invariant from HIR.
`inline_fixnum_inc()` now emits `RefineType<Fixnum>` before `FixnumAdd` when necessary.

The refinement does not need a runtime guard.
The intrinsic contract already guarantees the Fixnum type.

This change lets the `Array#each` continuation compile with generic entry types.

## Caller continuation

A handler can return through a Ruby frame that did not enter through a normal JIT call.
A normal JIT return cannot assume that this caller has a valid native return path.

The shared exception trampoline processes each returned frame:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    RUN["Run exception entry"] --> RESULT{"Result is Qundef?"}
    RESULT -->|Yes| VM["Return Qundef to the interpreter"]
    RESULT -->|No| FINISH{"Returned frame has FINISH?"}
    FINISH -->|Yes| RETURN["Return the result from vm_exec"]
    FINISH -->|No| PUSH["Push the result on the caller stack"]
    PUSH --> NEXT["Compile or reuse the caller continuation"]
    NEXT --> RUN
```

`exception_osr_entry()` writes the result to the caller stack and advances `cfp->sp`.
It then compiles or reuses the continuation at the caller's current PC.

The trampoline updates `CFP` and `SP`, then enters that continuation.
This loop keeps eligible caller frames in ZJIT.

## Safe fallback

ZJIT does not enter a frame with an escaped environment.
Exception entry requires an on-stack environment because it loads locals through the existing `EP`.

ZJIT also returns to the interpreter after these conditions:

- The native stack has insufficient space.
- Executable memory is unavailable.
- HIR compilation fails.
- A continuation cannot compile safely.
- JIT code returns `Qundef`.

The fallback preserves the existing interpreter behavior.

Fixes Shopify/ruby#966.

## Performance

I compared `43b07929b0` with the complete branch on an Apple M5 Pro.
The base commit does not compile exception handlers.

Both builds used these commands:

```sh
./configure --enable-yjit --enable-zjit --disable-install-doc
make -j8
```

Each result uses the geometric mean from seven paired runs.
Each run used 20 warmup iterations and at least 50 measured iterations across eight seconds.

| Benchmark | Base | This change | Result | 95% confidence interval |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `liquid-compile` | 18.214 ms | 17.491 ms | 4.0% faster | 1.9% to 5.8% faster |
| `liquid-render` | 34.034 ms | 30.702 ms | 9.8% faster | 5.6% to 13.8% faster |
| `sequel` | 24.068 ms | 24.470 ms | 1.7% slower | 2.6% faster to 5.8% slower |

The `sequel` interval includes no change.

One additional run produced these ZJIT counters:

| Counter | Base | This change | Difference |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `exit_exception_handler` | 1,240,504 | 0 | Removed |
| `side_exit_count` | 1,578,510 | 561,219 | 64.4% lower |
| `exit_guard_type_failure` | 105,478 | 105,483 | No material change |
| `compiled_iseq_count` | 403 | 450 | 47 more ISEQs |
| `failed_iseq_count` | 0 | 0 | No failures |
| `code_region_bytes` | 2,637,824 | 2,916,352 | 10.6% larger |

Generic entries remove the exception-handler exit bottleneck without adding entry type guards.

## Verification

- `make zjit-check` passed all 1,969 Rust tests, with one skipped test.
- The same command passed 26 CLI tests and 7,605 assertions.
- The multi-PC example returned `[:left, :left, :right, :left, :right]`.
- The typed-local example returned `[18, 18, 18]`.

focused.body: We now materialize the necessary frames and call vm_throw directly. This is a minor performance win, but we can now inline BlockIseqDirect blocks that use the `throw` instruction (break/return).

focused.title: ZJIT: Specialize polymorphic class + monomorphic shape
focused.body:
If we have dispatch where the receiver is polymorphic in a class, right
now we just break up the dispatch by the class. This unfortunately leads
to polymorphic `attr_reader` being completely unspecialized by shape.

In this commit, make sure we, for each polymorphic branch, filter the
profiled types by the receiver's specialized class. That way we still
get a chance at monomorphizing by shape and specializing `attr_reader`
away.
